title: Lula Overturns Bolsonaro and Sends Brazilian Assets Sliding Into a Central Bank Week
subhead: Lula's runoff win sets up a fiscal fight with an 82.9% debt load and wiped 18% off Brazil ETF exposure in overnight trading, while traders open Fed, ECB and BoJ week with Brent above $115 and French 10-year yields still near 5%.

sections.heading: Brazil Reprices a Regime, Not an Election
sections.body:
Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won Brazil's presidency for the fourth time, taking 51.8% of valid votes to Flavio Bolsonaro's 48.2%, per the Superior Electoral Court. It is the first time since Brazil's 1989 return to direct elections that a candidate has won a runoff after losing the first round. Bolsonaro refused to concede and said he will seek annulment of the result, according to Reuters.

The market answer was immediate and brutal: the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ) fell as much as 20% in overnight trading, last down 18%. ING's Chris Turner had forecast a rally in both the real and local bonds on a Bolsonaro win, citing fiscal austerity and deregulation — that trade is now dead. The fiscal arithmetic the market is pricing: gross debt hit 82.9% of GDP in August, the highest since March 2021, per Central Bank of Brazil data, and Lula will govern with Bolsonaro's Liberal Party holding the largest congressional bench in decades.

There is a Latin American pattern worth naming. Lula's win blocks the rightward shift Trump had backed, and it lands the same weekend Serbia's Aleksandar Vucic conceded to a student-led movement after 14 years. Two incumbents or incumbent-aligned forces losing within 24 hours, in two very different economies, points to the same underlying pressure: cost of living and legitimacy, not ideology.
sections.whyItMatters: Brazil is the EM carry trade's biggest liquid position. A 20% single-day hit to the equity proxy means leveraged real and local-rate positions get unwound this week regardless of what Brazil's fundamentals do — and that outflow will be read as an EM risk signal at a Fed meeting where a hold is 90% priced.

sections.heading: Three Central Banks, One Question: Who Blinks on Credibility
sections.body:
The Fed decides Wednesday, the ECB Thursday, the BoJ Friday — the densest policy week since the summer. Fed funds futures price a 90% probability of a hold at 3.75%-4%, but the interesting part is the tail risk. Bank of America expects a quarter-point hike, calling it a heavy lift, and frames the stakes as a test of Chair Warsh's 'sea change' to forward guidance.

BofA economist Claudio Irigoyen put the trap in plain terms: 'If the Fed hikes, investors might worry about over tightening. If the Fed holds, markets could question the Fed's inflation-fighting credibility.' That is a credibility problem with no clean exit, and it is the reason every other asset this week is trading derivative to Wednesday's press conference.

China adds a separate variable: the Fifth Plenum is running alongside, and Asia opened mixed — Topix +0.37%, Nikkei -0.2%, Kospi -0.3%, Kosdaq -1.18%, ASX 200 -0.26%.
sections.whyItMatters: A hold with a hawkish Warsh presser is the base case, but BofA's hike call means the distribution has real tails. Whatever Warsh says Wednesday will set the dollar and the long end for the remainder of the quarter — and the ECB and BoJ then have to respond to a Fed they cannot predict.

sections.heading: Goldman Cuts Korea 25% and Still Says Buy
sections.body:
Goldman Sachs slashed its 12-month Kospi target to 9,000 from 12,000, citing volatility and slowing earnings momentum — while keeping an overweight. Strategists led by Timothy Moe note the index has fallen 40% from record highs and trades near four times earnings, roughly three standard deviations below its historical average.

The detail that matters for the AI trade: Goldman says valuations in Korea's memory chip sector imply a roughly 65% decline in 2027 earnings. Non-memory stocks, about half the index, are more than 30% undervalued by its estimate. Foreign investors, hedge funds especially, keep selling Korean and Taiwanese equities — South Korea has seen $1 billion in foreign outflows.

Goldman attributes the selloff to three things: doubts over AI spending sustainability, rising oil prices, and increasingly hawkish central banks. Those are exactly this week's three variables.
sections.whyItMatters: A bank cutting a target by a quarter and still calling 60%+ upside is telling clients the price is wrong but the timing is uninvestable. Memory-chip earnings are the cleanest read on whether the AI capex cycle is real — and the market is now pricing a 2027 collapse in them.

sections.heading: Oil Cools One Percent but the Supply Map Has Not Changed
sections.body:
Brent fell 1.31% to $115.19 and WTI slipped 1.5% to $101.83 in Asian trade Monday, after Brent settled Friday at $116.72 — a six-month high and a third straight weekly gain of 6.2%. WTI settled at $103.27, up 3.8% on the day and 2.3% on the week.

The driver is policy, not barrels. Saudi Arabia's coalition said it intercepted two drones, a ballistic missile and a cruise missile headed for Riyadh, plus 10 ballistic missiles aimed at the southern region, per Saudi Press Agency spokesman Turki Al-Maliki. The Houthis claimed seven operations including strikes on King Khalid International Airport and Saudi Aramco's Yanbu facilities. The airport, closed since an Oct. 10 strike that killed at least 13 and injured around 300, resumed operations Sunday using Terminals 1 and 2.

Underneath: Trump said the U.S. is not negotiating with Iran and something would happen 'fairly soon', U.S. officials told the New York Times that U.S.-Israeli strikes are planned after the Nov. 3 midterms, and DNI Jay Clayton circulated a memo saying Iran has 'substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel'. Energy Aspects' Amrita Sen: 'It's not a question of if. People are asking if it's a question of when.'
sections.whyItMatters: The one-day dip is noise against a market that has gained 6.2% in a week on strike timing. With the U.S. explicitly deferring action past Nov. 3, oil now carries an embedded post-election option — which means every barrel is partly a bet on the second week of November.

sections.heading: Moody's Buys France Three Weeks, the Streets Take It Back
sections.body:
France's 10-year yield settled around 5.03% Friday after breaching 5% for the first time since 2002 earlier in the week. Moody's held its Aa3 rating and negative outlook, saying a 'significant and sustained fiscal effort will still be needed beyond the presidential elections of April and May 2027' to stabilise a debt burden it projects will exceed 120% of GDP in 2027. There was a conditional carrot: an upgrade to stable if institutions can cut the deficit.

The reprieve is thin. For a second straight weekend, protests over cost of living and inequality turned violent — the Interior Ministry counted 410,000 demonstrators; riot police fired tear gas and water cannon in Paris, and looting hit Marseille and Lyon. The violence was less severe than the previous week but structurally identical.

The market question is whether the French premium is idiosyncratic or systemic — CNBC reports investors fear contagion into the rest of the euro zone.
sections.whyItMatters: Moody's has effectively extended France's deadline past its own 2027 election, which removes any near-term forcing mechanism for fiscal repair while keeping the 5% yield. That combination — no catalyst, no credibility — is what makes a spread stay wide rather than mean-revert.

sections.heading: Beijing's Tax Net Pushes Chinese Wealth Into the One Jurisdiction It Cannot Reach
sections.body:
The unintended consequence of Beijing's July 20% retroactive tax on income and gains from overseas trusts has been a flow into U.S. banks. Private bankers and lawyers in Singapore and Hong Kong tell CNBC that inquiries about opening U.S. accounts rose sharply, with some clients set up and funded in under two months — 'the hurdle is not that high,' said Keith Tan of Golden Acacia Capital.

The arbitrage is structural. The U.S. sits outside the OECD's Common Reporting Standard, the framework under which 100-plus jurisdictions automatically share account data. Singapore and Hong Kong banks are obliged to report China-linked accounts; American banks are not. Smaller accounts are going to regional banks and online brokers.
sections.whyItMatters: Capital controls are being defeated by a jurisdictional gap the U.S. has no incentive to close. Every dollar that leaves via this route is a dollar Beijing cannot tax, count, or repatriate — and it strengthens the dollar's role as the default store of unreported wealth precisely as dedollarization stories dominate the narrative.

sections.heading: Audi Puts $4 Billion in Georgia and Admits the Tariff Math
sections.body:
Audi will build its first U.S. plant in Georgia for $4 billion, announced by Trump at a rally ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms. CEO Gernot Dollner's justification was unusually candid: U.S. tariffs cost Audi 1.2 billion euros ($1.4 billion) last year because it imports every U.S.-market vehicle from Europe or Mexico. Tariffs on German vehicles are currently 15%, down from 25%.

Dollner said more than 70 sites were evaluated over a three-year process and that the timing coinciding with a political rally was, in his words, 'by coincidence'. The plant lands during a VW group restructuring that includes 50,000 job cuts and four German plant closures, including an Audi facility, between 2031 and 2034.
sections.whyItMatters: This is tariff policy converting trade flows into fixed capital — the irreversible kind. A $4 billion plant cannot be relocated if tariffs fall, which means German industrial capacity is now permanently migrating on the assumption that tariff walls stay up.

bottomLine: Brazil's election gave markets a clean, tradeable shock — a 20% overnight repricing of an $82.9% debt-to-GDP economy with no fiscal anchor and an opposition-majority Congress — and it arrives the same week the Fed, ECB and BoJ decide policy. Warsh faces the credibility trap BofA laid out: hold and look soft on inflation, hike and risk over-tightening. Oil sits at $115 with a post-Nov. 3 strike option embedded, Korea's memory complex is priced for a 65% 2027 earnings collapse, and French 10-year paper is holding near 5% with Moody's having just pushed the reckoning past 2027. Watch Wednesday's press conference, but the fastest-moving risk is EM: the Brazil unwind is the first real test of whether this cycle's carry trades can survive a political surprise.
sources: CNBC, Reuters, Superior Electoral Court of Brazil (TSE), Central Bank of Brazil, iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ), ING (Chris Turner), Bank of America (Claudio Irigoyen), Goldman Sachs (Timothy Moe), Saudi Press Agency, Saudi-led Coalition to Restore Legitimacy in Yemen (Turki Al-Maliki), Houthi military media (Telegram), Energy Aspects (Amrita Sen), Office of the Director of National Intelligence (Jay Clayton memo via New York Times), Moody's Investors Service, French Interior Ministry, Audi / Volkswagen Group (Gernot Dollner), Golden Acacia Capital (Keith Tan), OECD Common Reporting Standard
